name: Cauthorn-Wilson Couloir

pitch_detail.notes: From the basin east of the peak, climb the snow in the big couloir splitting the East Face up to where it pinches down. The snow firms up with height. On warm days meltwater can carve deep runnels, and the whole face takes sun early, so start at first light.

At the pinch, climb the waterfall on the right side of the couloir. Grades given for this pitch range from WI3 to WI3+. It ends at a fixed piton anchor at the foot of the crux pitch; back it up. A short step at its base shows the ice quality before committing.

Sustained WI4 for a stretch, then easing to about WI3+ before the ice lets out onto lower-angled snow. Once sun-baked the ice turns aerated and screws hold poorly; if it looks that way from below, this is the place to turn around.

From the top of the crux, three or four pitches of snow, ice or mixed ground lead to the ridgeline. Rock anchors, some fixed, and V-threads where ice allows let most parties rappel the line from the ridge with two 60 m ropes. The east face is avalanche-prone in warm weather.

Parties continuing to the true summit climb short pitches of about 5.4 rock from the ridgeline, then descend by the West Ridge rappel route instead of the couloir. Small rock gear and pitons are the useful pieces.

descent_text: Many teams choose to rappel back down the couloir/ridgeline itself, building anchors on rock (some pre-existing/fixed) or building V-threads in the ice where present. Parties who continue to the true summit instead descend via the standard West Ridge descent used by the rock routes.
approach:
This route is on the east face, so the approach is the South Buttress approach with one extra step. From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, take the cairned climbers' track from its east end, drop through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak.

From there, cross the rib that runs south from the South Buttress into the basin east of the peak. Once you are in the right basin there is no ambiguity about the line — the objective is the large couloir splitting the East Face, and it is the dominant gully on that aspect. The error to avoid here is a basin error, not a gully error.

Usually climbed soon after SR-20 reopens, typically April into May.
overview: Cutthroat's classic moderate ice line: a big, sun-exposed couloir on the East Face that climbs through a sustained WI4 crux pitch and several pitches of snow/ice/mixed terrain toward the summit ridge.
beta: Grade III, WI4. Roughly 400 ft of snow or névé leads to a WI3 ice step at the couloir's pinch, then a sustained WI4 crux pitch that eases to about WI3+, followed by three or four pitches of snow, ice or mixed ground to the ridgeline. An early-season route, best soon after SR-20 reopens; the east face takes sun for most of the day and is avalanche-prone in warm weather.
gear: 4-6 ice screws, including a couple of stubbies for thin ice near the top of the WI3-3+ pitch
2-3 knifeblade/Bugaboo pitons plus angle pitons #1-3 — thin, flaring cracks on the buttress protect better with pins than cams
Small cams to 1" and about 6 assorted nuts
Two 60m ropes — required for the rappel descent off the route
Helmet — this is an east-facing couloir that gets sun most of the day, so watch for rockfall/wet slides as it warms
fa: Dan Cauthorn and Tim Wilson, April 1984
